content.title: About
content.content: Bean paste, sweetened is a thick paste made from cooked beans and sweetened with sugar or other sweeteners. It is widely used in Asian cuisine, especially in Japanese, Korean and Chinese desserts, as well as in baking and sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally the paste is made from red azuki beans, but other bean varieties can be used.
In Japan the sweet bean paste is called “anko” and is considered a fundamental sweet ingredient.
The paste is often used as a filling for mochi, dango, rolls and bento boxes.
There are two main types: “tsuba‑anko” (coarse) and “kitsu‑anko” (smooth).
It can be stored in the refrigerator for several weeks and frozen for up to a year.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Beans provide a notable amount of protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and helps maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The paste contains thiamine, riboflavin and folate, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many sweet spreads, sweet bean paste is low in fat.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytochemicals in beans help combat free radicals.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The paste is often heavily sweetened, so people with diabetes or those monitoring sugar intake should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to beans, experiencing skin rashes, swelling or respiratory issues.

items.title: Phytic acid presence
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce the absorption of certain minerals; large amounts of paste should be balanced with other foods.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sweet bean paste is used as a filling for buns, rolls, pancakes and cakes, added to sauces, ice cream, or simply eaten by the spoonful as a dessert. It can be gently warmed to become more pliable.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the paste in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 weeks. For longer storage, freeze in small portions where it will retain quality for up to 12 months. Before use, check for any off‑smell indicating fermentation.
